h1: Wine and cash: why ageing ties up money
title: Why Wine Ageing Ties Up Cash | Craft Beer School
desc: Why a winery pays out at harvest and is paid months or years later, with a simple cash timeline and ways to shorten the gap.
teaser: You pay for the grapes in autumn. You may not be paid for the wine for a year or two.
standfirst: Wine is a slow product. Between picking and payment there is fermentation, settling, ageing and bottling. Every month of it is money tied up. Here is how to see the gap and plan for it.
sections: The cash gap in one picture

A beer brewer can turn raw materials into cash in weeks. A winery cannot. Grapes arrive once a year in a few weeks. They are paid for then. Labour, yeast, tank time and cellar costs follow. The wine then sits through fermentation, clarification and often months of ageing before it is bottled, labelled and sold.

The gap between paying for fruit and receiving payment for the bottle is the period your cash is locked into wine. For a simple fresh white it may be several months. For a red aged in oak, then in bottle before release, it can stretch beyond a year or two. Your exact timeline depends on the style you choose.

Beer fans see the contrast quickly. A tank of lager is cash in weeks. A tank of red may be cash next year. The same discipline applies to both, but the wine calendar leaves much less room to correct a mistake.
What actually ties up the money

Think of wine moving through stages, each holding value that was paid for in cash:

  • Fruit and juice in the tank: the grape cost plus harvest labour.
  • Wine in ageing: add tank or barrel time, cellar costs, losses and analysis.
  • Bottled wine: add glass, closure, label, carton and bottling labour.
  • Finished stock waiting for a buyer: all of the above with nothing coming in.

Stock on your books is real money you have spent. It only becomes cash when somebody pays for the bottle.

Suppose a winery spends 100 units on fruit and cellar costs in the autumn, then 30 units on bottling six months later. It sells the wine evenly over the next twelve months for a total of 220 units. Cash out reaches 130 before the first bottle is sold. Cash in builds up slowly. The business turns a profit of 90 units on paper but needs to fund 130 units of cash from the start.

These are made-up numbers to show the method. Replace them with your own and draw the same timeline by month.
Why ageing is also a quality choice

Some wines need time. Oak and bottle ageing can round tannins and develop flavour in styles built for it. Others are best young and fresh. Ageing a wine that does not benefit simply adds cost. Choose the release date for each wine on quality grounds first, then check the cash impact.

This is a good place to be honest with yourself. A style that needs two years before sale is a different business from one that sells in six months.

One practical test helps. Taste the wine at intervals and ask whether it is better than it was last month. If it has stopped improving, holding it longer only costs money. Keep a log of tasting notes by date so the decision rests on records rather than hope.

Oak adds cost too. A barrel is a capital item that holds wine for months, adds flavour and loses a little wine to evaporation. If your style does not need it, tanks and staves can do a lot of the work for less money.

• Make some early-release wines, such as a young white, rosé or a fruit wine, to bring cash in sooner.
  • Sell direct from the tasting room at full price. See tasting rooms as a business.
  • Offer a wine club or pre-release offer so customers pay before bottling. See our note on wine clubs.
  • Agree payment terms with shops and distributors, then chase them.
  • Pay growers on terms that match your cash, if they agree.

Each of these has a cost, whether margin, effort or relationship. Weigh them against the interest you would pay to borrow.

Working capital is the money that covers the gap. Many new wineries budget for the building and equipment and forget it. A lender will not. Build a monthly cash flow from harvest to the last bottle of the vintage and find the lowest point. That depth is how much working capital you need, plus a reserve for a slow sales year.

A wine lost to a fault is worse than a late payment, because you spent the cash and have nothing to sell. Keep a reserve for it. Our guide on funding a winery shows what lenders ask about this.

Update the cash timeline after every harvest and every bottling. Compare plan with what happened. Over a few vintages you learn your own cycle and can stop guessing.

Keep one sheet per vintage with the date and amount of every cost and every sale. After three vintages you will have your own average gap between pick and payment. That number is more useful than any industry rule of thumb.

It also makes conversations with a bank easier. A founder who can say how many months of cash each vintage locks up gets taken seriously.
faqs: Why is winery cash flow so slow?
Because wine is made once a year and often aged before sale. You pay for fruit and cellar work months or years before the bottle sells.
How much working capital does a winery need?
Build a monthly cash flow and find its lowest point. That figure plus a reserve is your answer. It depends on style, scale and sales speed.
No. Only styles built for it benefit. Otherwise it adds cost.
Can a fruit wine shorten the gap?
Often yes, because many fruit wines are released young. See our guide on starting a fruit wine business.
